group.passage:
For centuries, people have argued about what Stonehenge was for. Some have seen it as a temple, others as an observatory or a calendar that followed the sun, and it was also the largest burial ground in Britain of its time. Building on the site began about 5,000 years ago, and the monument kept changing for roughly two thousand years. Now the stones themselves are offering fresh clues.
The first stones raised at Stonehenge, around 3000 BCE, were 43 bluestones whose source, the Preseli Hills of west Wales, lies some 225 kilometers away. The much larger sarsens came from about 24 kilometers to the north. For about a century, experts believed that the six-tonne Altar Stone had also come from Wales. In 2024, however, scientists who examined the ages and chemistry of tiny mineral grains in pieces of the stone found that they matched rocks in northeast Scotland instead. The stone must have traveled at least 700 kilometers, farther than any other stone known from a monument of that age. Since the wheel had not yet reached Britain, moving such loads would have required hundreds or even thousands of people.
Why go to so much trouble? In a study published in December 2024, Mike Parker Pearson and his colleagues argue that Stonehenge was meant to bring people together. Of more than 900 stone circles in Britain, it is the only one whose stones all came from distant regions. The Altar Stone, which lies flat, also resembles the stones of a type of circle found only in northeast Scotland, so it may have been sent as a gift to strengthen an alliance. Other evidence points the same way: people from many parts of Britain brought pigs and cattle to winter feasts at nearby Durrington Walls, and close to half of those buried at Stonehenge had spent part of their lives elsewhere. The second main stage of building, around 2500 BCE, came as newcomers from what are now the Netherlands and Germany arrived with metalworking skills, and the researchers suggest the monument may have been a way to unite the native Britons.
The idea is still a theory, and many questions remain. As the researchers themselves note, such unity could have been achieved by force or by agreement, and no one yet knows exactly where in Scotland the Altar Stone came from or how it was moved. Stonehenge may well have served several purposes at once.

translation_zh.text:
幾百年來，人們一直爭論巨石陣究竟有什麼用途。有人認為它是神殿，有人認為它是天文臺，或是追蹤太陽的曆法；它也是當時不列顛最大的墓地。這個地點的建造始於大約 5,000 年前，此後約兩千年間，這座建築不斷改變。現在，石頭本身正提供新的線索。
大約西元前 3000 年，巨石陣最早豎立的是 43 塊藍石，它們的產地——威爾斯西部的普雷塞利山——距離這裡約 225 公里。大得多的砂岩巨石則來自北方約 24 公里處。大約一個世紀以來，專家都相信重達六公噸的祭壇石也來自威爾斯。然而在 2024 年，科學家檢驗了這塊石頭碎片中微小礦物顆粒的年代與化學成分，發現它們和蘇格蘭東北部的岩石相符。這塊石頭一定走了至少 700 公里，比當時任何一座建築所用的已知石頭都遠。由於輪子當時還沒傳到不列顛，搬運這麼重的東西需要成百甚至上千人。
為什麼要這麼大費周章？在 2024 年 12 月發表的研究中，麥克‧帕克‧皮爾森和同事主張，巨石陣是為了把人們團結在一起而建的。在不列顛九百多座石圈中，只有它的石頭全都來自遠方。平躺的祭壇石也很像一種只見於蘇格蘭東北部的石圈中的石頭，所以它可能是一份禮物，用來鞏固雙方的結盟。其他證據也指向同一方向：不列顛各地的人帶著豬和牛到附近的杜靈頓牆參加冬季宴會，而且葬在巨石陣的人有將近一半曾在別處生活過一段時間。大約西元前 2500 年的第二個主要建造階段，正好是來自今日荷蘭與德國的新移民帶著金屬加工技術到來的時候；研究人員認為，這座建築可能是團結當地不列顛人的一種方式。
這個想法仍然只是理論，還有許多問題有待解答。研究人員自己也指出，這樣的團結可能是靠武力達成，也可能是靠協議；而且至今沒有人知道祭壇石確切來自蘇格蘭的哪裡，或它是怎麼被搬運的。巨石陣很可能同時具有好幾種用途。

problems: 第二段首句「The first stones raised at Stonehenge, around 3000 BCE, were 43 bluestones」把事實單 f3 的兩件事合成一句：f3 說最早豎立的是藍石、現有藍石 43 塊，但沒有說約西元前 3000 年豎立的正好是 43 塊（43 是現存藍石數，第一階段豎立的數目並不確定）。來源 Aberystwyth（s2）的寫法相近（43 bluestones were brought…；first stage … bluestones were erected），不影響任何小題，列 warn 供人工審核；之後改版可寫成 bluestones, 43 of which still stand at the site
